lessonActivities.title: Also: Adding Information the Right Way ➕
lessonActivities.content:
Also means "in addition." It is used in positive sentences to add an agreeing thought. ➕

Position rules:

  • After "to be": I am also Canadian. She was also there.
  • Before other verbs: I also sing. He also helped us.
  • Between auxiliary and verb: I have also been to Hong Kong. I can also speak French.

Not only... but also:

  • She not only sings but she also plays the piano.

Fun fact: Also is the most flexible of the three adverbs in terms of position! 🎯
functions: Adding agreeing thoughts in positive sentences
lessonActivities.tips: 💡 Quick Rule: Also comes after 'to be' and before other verbs.

lessonActivities.title: Too: Agreeing at the End 👍
lessonActivities.content:
Too means "in addition" and usually comes at the end of a clause. 👍

Standard position:

  • I am Canadian too.
  • I can speak French too.
  • I am studying economics too.

After the subject (formal):

  • Mr. Jones wanted the contract. Ms. Jackson, too, thought it was necessary.
  • Donna is working on a solution. I, too, am trying to find a way.

Short responses:

  • A: Enjoy Thanksgiving. B: You too!

Fun fact: Too comes from Old English "to" meaning "in addition"! 📜
functions: Using too in formal and informal contexts
lessonActivities.tips: 💡 Memory trick: Too is never at the beginning of a sentence. It likes the end!

lessonActivities.title: As well: Another Way to Say Too 🔄
lessonActivities.content:
As well means "in addition" and goes at the end of a clause, just like too. 🔄

Examples:

  • Harry likes pasta, and I like it as well.
  • You look tired, and I imagine you are hungry as well.
  • Sam visited the house with me, and the children came with us as well.

As well as:

  • She speaks French as well as German. (this is a different meaning!)

Fun fact: As well is slightly more common in British English than in American English! 🇬🇧
examples: I will have chicken, and vegetables as well.
She sings and plays guitar as well.
functions: Using as well as an alternative to too
Keeping as well at the end
lessonActivities.tips: 💡 Rule: As well and too are interchangeable at the end of clauses.

lessonActivities.title: Either: Negative Additions ➖
lessonActivities.content:
Either is used in negative sentences to add an agreeing thought. ➖

Examples:

  • Jane does not speak French. Sam does not speak French either.
  • I do not love chocolate. I do not love pizza either.
  • I cannot speak French either.

Position: Either goes at the end of the clause.

Neither alternative:

  • She does not like coffee. Neither do I. (more formal)

Fun fact: Either comes from Old English meaning "both" or "each of two"—now it is strictly for negatives! 🎓
lessonActivities.tips: 💡 Never forget: Either = negative. Too/Also = positive. Never use either in positive sentences.

lessonActivities.title: Also vs Too vs As well: What's the Difference? ⚖️
lessonActivities.content:
Let us compare all three side by side! ⚖️

AlsoTooAs well
Flexible positionEnd of clauseEnd of clause
Can start a sentenceCannot startCannot start
I also like pizza.I like pizza too.I like pizza as well.

Key differences:

  • Also: before verb, after be, between aux and verb, or at the start
  • Too: end of clause (or after subject with commas)
  • As well: end of clause only

Fun fact: In very formal writing, also is preferred over too and as well! 🎩
examples: As well: I like pizza as well.
functions: Choosing the correct word for the sentence structure
lessonActivities.tips: 💡 Decision point: If you want to start a sentence, use Also. If you want to end a sentence, use Too or As well.

lessonActivities.title: Also at the Start: Like Moreover 📝
lessonActivities.content:
Also can be put at the beginning of a clause to add information, like "moreover" or "furthermore." 📝

Examples:

  • Eva is a very good skier. Also, she goes hiking a lot.
  • Take warm clothes with you. Also, walking shoes are advised.
  • The insurance covered the damage to the car. Also, a replacement car was provided.

Important: Use a comma after also when it starts a sentence!

Fun fact: This use of also is very common in academic and business writing! 📊
examples: The insurance covered the damage. Also, a replacement car was provided.
She speaks French. Also, she knows German.
functions: Using also as a sentence adverb
lessonActivities.tips: 💡 Rule: When also starts a sentence, it acts like a transition word. Put a comma after it.

lessonActivities.title: Avoid These Common Errors ❌
lessonActivities.content:
Let us master the most common errors with these adverbs! ❌

Common mistakes:

  • ❌ Too, I would like to add something. → ✅ I would like to add something too.
  • ❌ As well, Peter would like to join. → ✅ Peter would like to join as well.
  • ❌ I like pizza also. (awkward at end) → ✅ I also like pizza. / I like pizza too.
  • ❌ I do not like it too. → ✅ I do not like it either.

Remember:

  • Too and as well NEVER start a sentence.
  • Also rarely goes at the very end.
  • Either = negative. Too/Also = positive.

Fun fact: These errors are so common that examiners specifically test for them! 🎯
examples: ❌ Too, I would like to add something. → ✅ I would like to add something too.
❌ I do not like it too. → ✅ I do not like it either.
lessonActivities.tips: 💡 Remember: Too and as well NEVER start a sentence. Also rarely goes at the very end.

lessonActivities.title: Formal & Informal Usage 🎩
lessonActivities.content:
Let us explore formal and informal usage! 🎩

Informal:

  • I like it too.
  • Me too!

Formal:

  • I, too, believe this is correct.
  • Mr. Smith, too, supported the proposal.
  • Also, previous studies have shown consistent results.

Academic writing:

  • Prefer also or moreover at the beginning.
  • Avoid too and as well in formal essays.

Fun fact: The formal "I, too" with commas was extremely common in 19th-century literature! 📖
examples: Formal: I, too, am concerned about this issue.
functions: Adapting to formal and informal registers
Using commas correctly with formal too
lessonActivities.tips: 💡 Master level: 'I, too,' with commas around it is formal and elegant. Use it in essays and professional emails.

writingActivities.question: Write about your skills and hobbies using also. Include at least 2 sentences with also in different positions (before a verb, after be, or between auxiliary and verb).
writingActivities.hint: Use also correctly: I also play tennis. I am also a musician. I have also visited Spain.

writingActivities.question: Write agreeing statements using too, as well, and either. Include 1 positive sentence with too or as well, and 1 negative sentence with either.
writingActivities.hint: Positive: I like it too. Negative: I don't like it either. Remember: either is for negatives!
sentenceStarters: I like ___, and I like ___ too
She doesn't ___, and I don't ___ either

writingActivities.question: Combine information about two people using also, too, and as well. Write at least 3 sentences showing different positions.
writingActivities.hint: Example: John plays football. He also plays basketball. His sister plays too. They both play tennis as well.

writingActivities.question: Write a short paragraph starting two sentences with Also to add extra information (like moreover).
writingActivities.hint: Use Also, at the beginning of a sentence with a comma. Example: Take an umbrella. Also, wear comfortable shoes.

writingActivities.question: Write two sentences: one informal using too at the end, and one formal using I, too, with commas.
writingActivities.hint: Informal: I want to go too. Formal: I, too, would like to attend the meeting.

writingActivities.question: Write three negative agreeing sentences using either. Show that you and others don't do something.
writingActivities.hint: Use either at the end of negative sentences. Example: I don't eat meat. My brother doesn't eat meat either.

gameActivities.question: Choose the correct position for also:
gameActivities.sentence: She sings and she ____ plays the piano.
gameActivities.hint: Before the main verb, use also. Too and as well go at the end.

gameActivities.question: Which word fits best in this negative sentence?
gameActivities.sentence: I don't like coffee, and I don't like tea ____.
gameActivities.hint: In negative sentences, use either at the end. Too and as well are for positive sentences.

gameActivities.question: Advanced: Choose the most formal option:
gameActivities.sentence: The manager approved the plan. ____, the director agreed.
gameActivities.hint: Only Also can start a sentence to add information like 'moreover'. Too and As well cannot start sentences.

quizActivities.question: Where does also usually go with verbs other than be?
quizActivities.hint: With verbs other than be, also comes immediately before the main verb.
quizActivities.explanation: Also comes before the verb: I also sing. She also plays.

quizActivities.question: Where does too usually go?
options: At the end of a clause
quizActivities.correctAnswer: At the end of a clause
quizActivities.hint: Too typically occupies the final position in a clause.
quizActivities.explanation: Too usually comes at the end: I like it too. I am happy too.

quizActivities.question: Which is used in negative sentences?
quizActivities.hint: Only either is used to agree with negative statements.
quizActivities.explanation: Either is used in negative sentences. Too, also, and as well are for positive sentences.

quizActivities.question: Choose the correct sentence:
quizActivities.hint: Too goes at the end of the clause.
quizActivities.explanation: Too goes at the end: I like pizza too. 'I too like pizza' is possible but formal and requires commas.

quizActivities.question: Which sentence uses also correctly?
quizActivities.hint: Also goes before the main verb.
quizActivities.explanation: Also goes before the verb: She also speaks French. After be: She is also French.

quizActivities.question: Complete the negative sentence:
quizActivities.hint: Negative sentences use either at the end.
quizActivities.explanation: In negative sentences, either goes at the end: I don't like it either.

quizActivities.question: Which can start a sentence?
quizActivities.sentence: Choose the word that can begin a sentence.
quizActivities.hint: Only also can function as a sentence starter meaning 'moreover'.
quizActivities.explanation: Also can start a sentence: Also, we need to consider the costs. Too and as well cannot start sentences.

quizActivities.question: Complete the sentence:
quizActivities.hint: Positive sentence at the end of a clause.
quizActivities.explanation: Too goes at the end of positive clauses: I am Canadian too.

quizActivities.question: Which is formal?
quizActivities.hint: Commas around too after the subject indicate formal usage.
quizActivities.explanation: 'I, too, agree' with commas around too is formal. 'I agree too' is informal.

quizActivities.question: Complete the sentence:
quizActivities.sentence: She not only sings ____ she also plays piano.
quizActivities.hint: The correlative conjunction is 'not only... but also'.
quizActivities.explanation: The correct pattern is 'not only... but also': She not only sings but she also plays piano.

quizActivities.question: Identify the error:
quizActivities.sentence: As well, I would like to join.
quizActivities.hint: As well cannot start a sentence.
quizActivities.explanation: As well cannot start a sentence. Use Also: Also, I would like to join.

quizActivities.question: Complete the sentence:
quizActivities.sentence: Jane speaks French. Sam speaks French ____.
quizActivities.hint: Positive agreement at the end of the clause.
quizActivities.explanation: Too adds positive agreement at the end: Sam speaks French too.

quizActivities.question: Which sentence is correct?
quizActivities.hint: Also goes before the main verb want.
quizActivities.explanation: Also goes before the main verb: I also want to go. Between auxiliary and verb: I have also wanted to go.

quizActivities.question: Complete the negative sentence:
quizActivities.sentence: He doesn't study, and he doesn't work ____.
quizActivities.hint: Negative agreement requires either at the end.
quizActivities.explanation: Either is used for negative agreement at the end of the clause.

quizActivities.question: Advanced: Which shows the most formal usage?
options: Mr. Smith, too, supported the proposal
Mr. Smith supported the proposal too
Mr. Smith also supported the proposal
Also Mr. Smith supported the proposal
quizActivities.correctAnswer: Mr. Smith, too, supported the proposal
quizActivities.hint: Formal too appears after the subject surrounded by commas.
quizActivities.explanation: 'Mr. Smith, too, supported' with commas is the most formal. 'Also' is formal but 'too' with commas is the most sophisticated.

spellingActivities.hint: Used to add an agreeing thought in positive sentences
spellingActivities.sentence: She not only sings but she also plays the piano.

spellingActivities.hint: Used in negative sentences to add an agreeing thought
spellingActivities.sentence: I don't like coffee, and I don't like tea either.

spellingActivities.hint: Formal synonym for also - used to add information across sentences
spellingActivities.sentence: Additionally, we need to consider the costs.
